prime.problem: '68–95–99.7' gets quoted for everything, but it is the normal's answer. For a skewed discrete distribution the true coverage at 1σ can be 0.547 or 0.867, and Chebyshev's guarantee is too loose to be useful.
prime.fits: The last card. It lines up the six families you have now met (uniform, binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, geometric, negative binomial) against the normal and Chebyshev, so it works as a comparison across the whole distributions part.
expect: P(|X − μ| < kσ) as a finite sum
prime.goal: Compute the exact kσ coverage of any discrete distribution, and explain why it differs from the normal's.

attend: Why does Poisson(4) drop to 0.547 at k = 1 while the others don't?
Why do the skewed distributions cover more than the normal at k = 1 but less at k = 3?
Why do switching the geometric's convention, or counting the other colour, leave the coverage unchanged?
Which three-point distribution makes Chebyshev's bound exact, and why does that mean it can't be improved?

must: Only whole numbers carry probability → coverage = Σ p(x) over the integers strictly inside (μ − kσ, μ + kσ) → it jumps whenever an edge crosses an integer → Poisson(4)'s edges land exactly on 2 and 6, and strict < drops both → 0.547 (0.798 with ≤)
A long one-sided tail → inflates σ → ±σ swallows the whole short side (geometric: 1..7, 0.867) → but the tail still reaches past 3σ → 0.982, below the normal's 0.9973
Chebyshev uses only μ and σ → it must hold for the worst case (all the mass at ±k) → 1 − 1/k² (0 at k = 1, 0.75 at k = 2) → always true, rarely tight
Shift or reflect X (trials against failures, X against 5 − X) → μ and the interval move with it → the same bars stay inside → the same coverage
elevated: Compare squares as Fractions, (x − μ)² < k²σ² → exact ties are decided correctly → a float σ could round Poisson's edge bars either way

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences why the six distributions don't follow 68–95–99.7, naming the lattice effect and the skew effect with one example each.
checklist: coverage is a sum over the integers strictly inside the interval
lattice: an edge landing on an integer makes < against ≤ matter (Poisson(4): 0.547 against 0.798)
skew: a long tail inflates σ, raising coverage at k = 1 and lowering it at k = 3
Chebyshev is the floor for any distribution; the normal is just one case
shifting or reflecting X doesn't change coverage

retrieve.q: Explain why the 68–95–99.7 rule is only an approximation for these six, and which of them come closest.
answer: it is the normal's coverage, erf(k/√2)
discrete lattices and skew both move the answer
the binomial and hypergeometric, which are fairly symmetric with many values, land within 0.02 at k = 1

retrieve.q: Trace the Binomial(10, 0.6) row at k = 1: μ, σ, the interval, the integers inside and the sum.
Quote 68–95–99.7, use Chebyshev, simulate, or sum the pmf: when is each acceptable?
answer: 68–95–99.7: for a rough sense when the distribution is close to normal
Chebyshev: when all you know is μ and σ and you need a guarantee
simulation: a check with about ±0.0005 error at 10⁶ draws, which still needs an explicit tie rule
summing the pmf: whenever you have it; exact, with at most 14 terms here

compare.q: Poisson(4) and Geometric(0.25) both have mean 4. Why do they sit at the two ends of the k = 1 range, 0.547 and 0.867?
answer: Poisson(4): σ = 2 puts both edges exactly on integers, and the strict rule drops two tall bars
Geometric(0.25): σ = 3.46, inflated by the long tail, so the band covers everything from 1 to 7
same mean, different shape and σ, very different coverage

compare.q: This card's discrete coverage against the normal and Chebyshev in cs-9: what does a continuous distribution remove, and what stays?
answer: continuous: no lattice jumps, and < against ≤ doesn't matter
what stays: the shape still decides coverage, and Chebyshev is still the floor
the normal's 68.27 / 95.45 / 99.73% is exact only for the normal

predict.q: Poisson(9): μ ± σ = 9 ± 3 lands exactly on 6 and 12. Predict the strict and the ≤ coverage at k = 1, and which is closer to 0.6827. Commit first.
predict.answer: Strict (7…11): 0.5962. With ≤ (6…12): 0.7601. Neither is close: the normal's 0.6827 sits between them, because the two edge bars carry about 0.16 of the mass. A bigger λ doesn't make the lattice jump go away.

apply.task: Add Binomial(20, 0.5) to the zoo: work out μ, σ and the integers inside at k = 1 and k = 2, then compute the coverage with coverage. Predict first: is it closer to the normal than Binomial(10, 0.6)?
apply.done: μ = 10 and σ = √5 ≈ 2.236. At k = 1 it keeps 8…12, coverage 0.7368; at k = 2 it keeps 6…14, 0.9586. It is further from 0.6827 at k = 1 than Binomial(10, 0.6)'s 0.6665: a symmetric shape with more trials doesn't remove the lattice effect, because the band 7.76–12.24 happens to take in 5 whole bars.
apply.hint: The pmf is comb(20, x) * F(1, 2**20), with μ = F(10) and var = F(5).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: Poisson(9)'s two coverages, or whether Binomial(20, 0.5) gets closer to the normal?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why skew raises coverage at k = 1 but lowers it at k = 3, or why Chebyshev can't be improved?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: edge on an integer → a jump in coverage, or tail → larger σ → a wider band?
Which of the six families could you now rebuild from memory (pmf, mean, variance) to redo a row?
What will you revisit before cs-9's normal and Chebyshev card?
